extracted.intended_audience: readers, students, and translators of classical Latin lyric poetry (Horace)
extracted.subtask_description: English translations of Horace's Odes (Third Book) intended for reading, study, or translation; contains lyric poems that exemplify Horace's poetic principles and usages. Useful for literary analysis, translation practice, and understanding classical poetic voice and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of tone and style to subject
rubrics_metrics.description: "These themes ill suit the merry lyre. Whither, muse, are you going?--Cease, impertinent, to relate the language of the gods, and to debase great things by your trifling measures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match poetic tone, meter, and manner to the gravity of the subject. Do not treat lofty or serious themes with an inappropriately light, jocular, or trivial style; avoid 'debas[ing] great things by... trifling measures.' Anti-pattern: pairing lofty mythic or tragic material with a levity that undermines its dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and reserved delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: "Preserve a religious silence: I, the priest of the Muses, sing to virgins and boys verses not heard before."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value novelty and discretion: cultivate fresh material and avoid merely repeating familiar or hackneyed verses. The poet should be deliberate about when and to whom to present work ('preserve a religious silence') — implying restraint in composition and presentation. Example practice: aim to sing 'verses not heard before.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and moderation over ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Since then nor Phrygian marble, nor the use of purple more dazzling than the sun, nor the Falernian vine, nor the Persian nard, composes a troubled mind... why should I set about a lofty edifice with columns that excite envy... Why should I exchange my Sabine vale for wealth, which is attended with more trouble?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer restraint, modesty, and simplicity rather than excessive ornament, grandiosity, or costly display. In poetic practice this favors clear, measured expression and subject-matter grounded in modest life over overwrought or ostentatious elaboration that may distract or create trouble. Anti-pattern: excessive rhetorical show that obscures meaning or causes strain on the poet/subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor voice and invocation to audience/patron
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent direct addresses and invocations throughout the book (e.g., "TO MAECENAS," "Descend from heaven, queen Calliope," "O Maecenas, learned in both languages").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate persona, addressee, or invocation to frame the poem and to establish tone, purpose, and social context. Invoking a muse or addressing a patron can set expectations for subject, register, and rhetorical stance; use these devices deliberately to position the poem for its intended audience.
